shared_text:
The flight. A narrow-body airliner landing at an airport at night. Visual conditions.

The crew. The first officer was the pilot flying and the captain the pilot monitoring. The captain had 7,750 hours, 1,600 of them on type, and 225 hours in the previous 90 days. The crew were tired and had little experience of operating at the airport.

What happened. The runway was in use for both landings and departures. The aircraft was light, at about 57.5 tonnes, with an approach speed of about 122 knots and a headwind of about 15 knots. The landing roll was very short, and the aircraft was at taxi speed between two exits early in the roll. There was traffic behind, and the crew judged it best to leave the runway at the next exit rather than continue at taxi speed to an exit further down the runway. The airport chart did not mark this exit as a hot spot. As the aircraft was already turning onto the exit, the tower controller told the crew to continue down the runway and leave at the next exit on the right. The turn had already been made, and it was not possible to turn back onto the runway. The controller then told the crew to hold short of a parallel taxiway, because aircraft were taxiing along it towards the runway for departure. The crew stopped the aircraft as instructed, still on the runway.
safe_outcome: The tower controller instructed the aircraft landing behind to go around. No one was hurt and no aircraft was damaged.
bad_outcome: The landing aircraft's crew saw the conflict late and went around from about 50 feet, passing low over this aircraft. A flight attendant on the landing aircraft was thrown off balance by the abrupt go-around and received a minor injury.
notes: Variant B-landing: the conflicting traffic was the aircraft landing behind, which ATC sent around; the departing aircraft on the taxiway were taxiing, not taking off. Bracket 'this aircraft': the aircraft was stopped still on the runway. Removed under rule 3: the Suggestions (designate a hot spot at that exit) and the note that an internal safety report was made. From the Contributing factors list, kept only the facts and states: tiredness, little experience at the airport, the low approach speed and short landing roll, and that the chart did not mark the exit as a hot spot; the list's causal framing was dropped. Moved to the safe ending under rule 5: the go-around of the following aircraft. Removed under rule 6: airport (named in the narrative, synopsis and airspace field), runway number, taxiway names and the departure point. Judgement calls: aircraft type coded only as 'Commercial Fixed Wing'; 'narrow-body airliner' inferred from the 57.5-tonne landing weight and 'Vapp'. The pilot flying is not named; the captain was pilot not flying, so the first officer is given as pilot flying. 'Fatigued' is unattributed in the report and rendered as 'the crew were tired'. Light coded as Night with a 0601-1200 time band; given as 'at night'. 'Land very short' is read as a very short landing roll (the aircraft was at taxi speed early), not a touchdown short of the runway.
